questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: Your PR reviewer runs with claude -p and, besides posting findings, has permission to commit fixes directly to the PR branch. Last sprint 3 of 40 auto-commits changed behaviour: one "fix" for a flagged null check removed an intentional guard, and the author never noticed because the commit landed under the bot's name mid-review. You want to keep offering fixes. What design change addresses this?

options.text: Keep autonomous commits but require the reviewer to run the full test suite first and commit only when it is green, treating a passing run as the approval signal.
options.explanation: The removed guard already passed the suite, so a green run is not evidence that behaviour was preserved. Tests approve what they cover, not the author's intent; this keeps the bot deciding on its own and adds CI time without closing the gap that let the change through.

options.text: Have the reviewer post fixes as suggested-change blocks the author applies, and reserve committing for an explicit opt-in trigger such as a comment on the PR.
options.explanation: This keeps the value of generated fixes while moving the decision to the author: a suggestion is visible, attributable, and applied deliberately. An opt-in trigger still allows autonomous commits where the author wants them. It beats the other options because it bounds autonomy at the point where intent is unknowable to the bot.

options.text: Move fix generation to a separate subagent with a narrower prompt so the findings and the code changes come from independent contexts.
options.explanation: Independent contexts improve review quality, but the problem here is who decides, not how the fix was derived. A separate subagent would still commit a behaviour-changing fix under the bot's name with the author unaware; it adds cost and does not change the autonomy boundary.

options.text: Restrict the bot to committing only findings rated "low" severity, since higher-severity changes deserve author attention and low ones are safe.
options.explanation: Severity describes the impact of the finding, not the risk of the fix. A null-check cleanup is exactly the kind of "low" finding whose fix silently changed behaviour. Tying autonomy to severity would let the same class of commits continue while making the rule feel principled.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: Your reviewer runs after a gitleaks step. Last week a PR added an internal service token in a format the scanner has no rule for. The reviewer noticed it, posted an inline comment quoting the value with the advice "move this to an environment variable", and continued with fourteen style findings. The comment was visible to every member of the GitHub org for two days before anyone rotated the token. How should the reviewer behave when it finds a live credential?

options.text: Add "never quote secret values in comments" to the review prompt and keep the finding in the normal list, with severity set to critical so it stands out.
options.explanation: A prompt rule reduces the chance of echoing the secret but keeps the event inside the ordinary review flow: a critical finding among fourteen style notes waits for the author to read it, and nobody who can rotate the token is told. The exposure clock keeps running.

options.text: Add the internal token pattern to the gitleaks rules so the scanner blocks such PRs before the reviewer runs, and leave the reviewer's behaviour as it is.
options.explanation: Extending the scanner is worth doing, but it only covers formats someone has already written a rule for; the stem is about the case the scanner missed. It leaves the reviewer with the same behaviour the next time it is the only component that notices a leak.

options.text: Have the reviewer redact the value and post the finding as critical severity so the existing severity gate blocks the merge until the author removes it.
options.explanation: Redaction and a merge block are improvements, yet a pushed credential is compromised whether or not the PR merges. Blocking the merge is the wrong control for the actual risk, and the security team still learns about it only if the author acts.

options.text: Treat it as a hard stop: halt the review, fail the check with a generic message, and trigger the security escalation path without echoing the value.
options.explanation: A live credential is a finding where continuing the task is the wrong decision: the review's value is negligible next to the exposure, and the right recipient is the security on-call, not the PR author. Stopping, failing the check, and escalating through a defined path without echoing the value is the stop condition the agent needs; completing the review first is what caused the two-day delay.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: Your reviewer meets a PR that changes the retry count for payment webhooks from 5 to 2. No ticket is linked, the description says "cleanup", and neither diff nor tests reveal whether the change is intentional. The prompt currently forces every observation into a severity-rated finding, so this would post as "critical: reduced resilience" and block the merge. How should the reviewer handle observations where intent cannot be determined?

options.text: Post it as a question to the author citing the evidence, kept separate from defect findings and excluded from severity-based merge gates.
options.explanation: An unexplained behaviour change is worth surfacing, but as a question, not a verdict. Separating questions from defects keeps severity meaningful for gating while still getting the author to confirm intent. This beats suppressing it, mislabelling it, or spending turns trying to force a classification the evidence cannot support.

options.text: Suppress it: if the reviewer cannot establish a defect, posting anything adds to false positives and erodes trust in the reviewer.
options.explanation: Silently dropping it means a possibly accidental change to payment resilience ships with no one asked. False-positive discipline applies to asserted defects; a clearly labelled question is not a false positive, and this policy would hide exactly the class of change humans most want to see.

options.text: Rate it "medium" rather than "critical" so it appears in the review but does not block the merge, letting severity encode the uncertainty.
options.explanation: Using severity to express confidence corrupts the scale: a medium finding should mean medium impact, not "we are not sure". Developers then cannot trust severity for gating, and the reviewer still asserts a defect it cannot substantiate.

options.text: Have the reviewer search the tracker and git history with additional tools until it can classify the change, then post a finding.
options.explanation: Extra evidence gathering is reasonable, but the stem says there is no ticket and the description is uninformative, so more searching will not reveal intent. It still ends in a forced classification, at higher cost and latency per PR.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: Your CI test-generation step reports that it raised line coverage on the billing module from 61% to 79% over six weeks, and leadership wants to expand it to all services. A staff engineer samples 30 generated tests and finds that 18 either assert only that a function returns without throwing or snapshot the current output; a known rounding bug in applyDiscount is exercised by three of them and caught by none. How should the step's value be measured before expansion?

options.text: Require a minimum coverage gain per PR and track the module's coverage trend over time, since coverage is the metric the step was commissioned to move.
options.explanation: Coverage measures lines executed, not behaviour verified, which is exactly how 18 of 30 tests can raise it while catching nothing. Making the target a coverage gain rewards the agent for more of the same and hides the rounding bug behind a green number.

options.text: Ask a second Claude session to grade each generated test for meaningfulness on a 1 to 5 scale and report the average grade per module.
options.explanation: A model grading another model's tests for "meaningfulness" produces a plausible-looking score with no ground truth, and shares the generator's blind spots about what the code should do. It measures agreement between two Claude sessions, not defect detection.

options.text: Run mutation testing on the covered modules and measure how many injected faults the generated tests kill, compared with the existing suite.
options.explanation: The question is whether the generated tests detect faults, and mutation testing answers it directly: inject changes into the code and count how many the tests catch. Comparing kill rate with the existing suite shows the marginal value of the step, and the applyDiscount bug would surface as surviving mutants. It evaluates the outcome the step is meant to produce rather than a proxy.

options.text: Count assertions per generated test and reject tests with fewer than two, so trivially passing tests are filtered out before they are committed.
options.explanation: An assertion count is a proxy that is easy to satisfy without value: two toBeDefined checks pass the filter and a single precise equality assertion fails it. Snapshot tests carry one assertion that encodes the current, possibly buggy, output.

questions.scenario: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.question: A developer wants Claude Code to migrate 60 files from a deprecated moment API to date-fns overnight, unattended. The mapping is mechanical and documented in an internal guide. They propose running claude --dangerously-skip-permissions in their main working tree so nothing prompts them. How should the run be bounded?

options.text: Split the migration into 60 short interactive sessions, one file each with the default permission prompts, so that any single mistake stays contained to one file.
options.explanation: Sixty interactive sessions is not unattended, which was the whole point, and per-file sessions lose the shared understanding of the mapping that makes the migration consistent. Containment is real but bought by discarding the automation.

options.text: Accept skipping permissions but instruct in the prompt to touch only files that import moment and to run the test suite after each file.
options.explanation: Prompt instructions are a request, not a boundary; with permissions skipped in the main working tree, a misread instruction can modify or delete anything. The test run helps detect problems but nothing limits what an unattended session may do.

options.text: Run it in a dedicated git worktree with a permission allowlist for Edit and the test command, and use the resulting PR as the human review gate.
options.explanation: The worktree isolates the blast radius, the allowlist limits the agent to the actions the task needs without prompting, and the PR puts a human at the point where judgment matters. This gives an unattended run with enforced limits, which the other options either lack or achieve by removing the automation.

options.text: Run it with permissions skipped inside a plan-mode session first, then replay the approved plan in a second unattended session using the same flag.
options.explanation: A plan does not constrain execution; the second session is still unrestricted in the main tree and may deviate from the plan when files differ from expectations. Plan mode also does not need permissions skipped, since it does not write, so the first step adds nothing.

questions.scenario: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.question: While fixing a failing test in OrderTotalTest, Claude Code changed the expected value from 119.00 to 118.99 and reported success. The test was right; the rounding bug is in the code. The team wants Claude to keep fixing failing tests autonomously but never "fix" a test by changing what it asserts. Which stop condition belongs in the workflow?

options.text: Make failing tests the contract: if the only way to pass is changing an assertion, Claude stops and reports the conflict instead of editing.
options.explanation: This defines the exact boundary that was crossed and turns it into an explicit stop-and-report condition, so the agent stays autonomous on genuine code fixes and escalates only when the test and the code disagree. It preserves the ability to add or repair tests while making assertion changes a human decision.

options.text: Add a hook that blocks all edits to files under tests/, guaranteeing that test assertions can never be altered by the agent on its own.
options.explanation: A blanket block stops legitimate work too: writing new tests, fixing a genuinely broken fixture, or updating a test after an intended behaviour change. The boundary is about intent, whether the code or the expectation is wrong, and a path rule cannot express that.

options.text: Require Claude to run the full suite after every change and revert whenever the pass count decreases, so regressions cannot land.
options.explanation: The pass count increased here, so this check would have approved the bad edit. It guards against a different failure, breaking other tests, and gives no signal when an assertion is weakened to match buggy code.

options.text: Move test fixing into plan mode so the developer reviews and approves each proposed change before Claude applies it to the code.
options.explanation: Approving every fix removes the autonomy the team asked to keep and makes routine code fixes as expensive as the rare contested one. It solves the problem by putting a human on every decision rather than on the specific decision that needs one.

questions.scenario: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.question: Your team needs 12 new REST endpoints that all follow the pattern of the existing orders handler: validation, service call, error mapping, OpenAPI annotation. A developer proposes launching 12 subagents in parallel, one per endpoint, to finish in minutes. In a trial the results compiled but used three different error-mapping styles and two annotation formats. What approach fits?

options.text: Keep the parallel fan-out but give every subagent the full CLAUDE.md and a longer prompt describing the conventions in detail.
options.explanation: The divergence came from twelve independent inferences of the pattern, and prose conventions still leave room for twelve interpretations. More text raises cost per subagent without providing the one thing that would align them: a concrete, already-reviewed example to copy.

options.text: Launch the 12 subagents sequentially instead of in parallel so each can see the previous endpoint's output before generating its own.
options.explanation: Subagents do not inherit each other's context, so running them in sequence gives none of them the previous output unless it is passed explicitly. This loses the speed of fan-out while keeping the inconsistency, the worst of both.

options.text: Have one subagent generate all 12 endpoints in a single run so a single context holds the pattern, then review the whole batch.
options.explanation: A single context does improve consistency, but there is no checkpoint: if the pattern is misread on the first endpoint, all twelve are wrong the same way and the review lands on a large batch. Consistency without an early human check just makes errors uniform.

options.text: Generate one endpoint first, review it, then hand the reviewed file to the remaining runs as the exemplar to copy.
options.explanation: One reviewed exemplar anchors every subsequent generation to a concrete, approved artifact rather than to inferred conventions, so parallel runs stay consistent. It keeps the speed of fan-out, puts the human check where it is cheapest, and beats prose instructions because the model copies rather than interprets.

questions.scenario: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.question: Claude Code has spent 25 minutes on an intermittent ECONNRESET in an integration test. The transcript shows it alternating between two hypotheses: it adds a connection-pool timeout, the test still fails, it reverts and adds a retry wrapper, the test still fails, and it returns to the timeout. No hypothesis has been checked against evidence. How do you break the loop?

options.text: Run /compact to clear the accumulated failed attempts from context so Claude can approach the problem fresh.
options.explanation: Context pressure is not what drives this loop; the agent is editing before verifying. Compacting also blurs the record of what was already tried, which is the one useful thing the transcript contains, so the next attempt may repeat the same two edits.

options.text: Stop and require a reproduction first: make the failure deterministic, then state a hypothesis with evidence before any edit.
options.explanation: The loop exists because edits are being used as experiments against an intermittent failure, so no result confirms or refutes anything. Forcing reproduce, then hypothesis with evidence, then edit gives each step a verifiable outcome. It fixes the loop's structure rather than its inputs or its context.

options.text: Delegate the investigation to a fresh subagent with the same task description so an uncontaminated context can find the fix.
options.explanation: A new context running the same unstructured process will oscillate the same way, and it discards what has been learned. Delegation helps when the parent's context is the problem, not when the debugging method is.

options.text: Paste the full server logs and the pool library's source into the conversation so Claude has all the information it could need.
options.explanation: Missing information is not the failure mode; the agent never tested the information it had. A large paste fills context, pushes the transcript toward compaction, and still leaves the model free to guess-and-edit.

questions.scenario: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.question: Legal requires a new license header in every one of 3,100 source files across the monorepo, replacing three older header variants. A developer asks Claude Code to "update the headers" and watches it Read and Edit files one at a time; after 40 minutes it has finished 180 files and the session context is filling. What should the developer do?

options.text: Ask Claude to write and test a script that performs the replacement, run it, then use Claude to review the diff for edge cases.
options.explanation: The task is deterministic and repetitive, so the right agent output is a program, not 3,100 edits. A script finishes in seconds, applies one rule uniformly, and leaves the model for the judgment work: writing the script correctly and reviewing the odd files the script mishandled.

options.text: Split the remaining files across eight parallel subagents by directory so the same approach completes within the session limit.
options.explanation: Parallelism multiplies the cost of using a model as a text-replacement engine and invites eight slightly different interpretations of the header rules. It finishes sooner but is still the wrong tool for a mechanical transformation.

options.text: Run /compact at intervals and continue, since the task is mechanical and Claude has demonstrated it handles it correctly.
options.explanation: Compaction addresses context, not throughput: at the observed rate the remaining files take roughly eleven more hours of model turns. The task being mechanical is the argument against doing it turn by turn, not for it.

options.text: Switch to plan mode so Claude lists every affected file and the exact replacement, then approve the plan and execute it.
options.explanation: A plan enumerating 3,100 files is not reviewable, and executing it still means per-file edits at the same pace. Plan mode helps when the approach is uncertain; here the approach is obvious and the problem is the execution mechanism.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: You automated weekly dependency updates with an SDK agent that has Bash and Edit: it bumps versions, runs tests, and opens a PR that auto-merges when green. Last week it bumped an ORM from 5.x to 6.x; tests passed because the removed API was only exercised by production jobs, and two nightly jobs failed. What autonomy boundary would you set?

options.text: Require the agent to read each package's changelog before bumping and skip any update whose notes mention breaking changes.
options.explanation: This leaves the decision with the model and depends on changelogs being complete and clearly worded, which many are not. The agent remains fully autonomous over major upgrades; it is just asked to be more careful, which is not a boundary.

options.text: Remove auto-merge entirely so every dependency PR waits for a human reviewer, since the incident shows tests cannot catch every regression.
options.explanation: Most weekly bumps are patch releases where a green run is adequate evidence; forcing humans to review all of them creates queue fatigue and rubber-stamping. It responds to one risky class of change by giving up automation on every class.

options.text: Have the agent also run the nightly job suite before merging, closing the gap that let the ORM change through.
options.explanation: Extending coverage helps for this specific gap but the next major upgrade will find another one; test coverage is never a proof of compatibility. It also makes every bump slow and expensive when the concern applies only to majors.

options.text: Tier by risk: patch and minor bumps may auto-merge on green; major bumps open a PR with a migration summary and require human approval.
options.explanation: Semver already encodes the risk signal, so tiering puts the human exactly where breaking changes are expected and nowhere else. Routine bumps stay automatic, majors get a reviewed PR with context, and the boundary is enforced by version, not by the model's reading of a changelog.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Your codebase-exploration assistant fans every question out to six subagents (API, data, jobs, UI, infra, tests) and synthesizes their reports. Engineers like it for "how does checkout work end to end?" but complain that "what does normalizeSku return?" takes 90 seconds, costs about 40x a direct lookup, and the synthesis sometimes contradicts the one relevant subagent. What should change?

options.text: Keep the fan-out but cut each subagent's turn budget so simple questions return faster and cost less per question.
options.explanation: Six agents still run for a question one Grep answers, and the synthesis step that introduces contradictions is untouched. Smaller budgets also degrade the broad questions the engineers value, so it makes both cases worse to make one slightly cheaper.

options.text: Let the main agent answer directly with Grep and Read by default, and fan out to subagents only for questions spanning multiple areas.
options.explanation: Delegation should be proportional to the question. A single-symbol lookup is one tool call in the main context, with no synthesis to go wrong; cross-cutting questions still get the parallel exploration that works. This removes the overhead and the contradiction source for simple cases without giving up the multi-agent path.

options.text: Add a seventh "router" subagent that reads each question and picks which of the six should run, so irrelevant reports are never produced.
options.explanation: Routing removes irrelevant reports but keeps a full delegation round-trip plus synthesis for a question the main agent could answer itself. It adds a model call and latency in front of every question, including the trivial ones.

options.text: Replace the six area subagents with one general explorer subagent so every question yields exactly one report for the coordinator to synthesize.
options.explanation: One subagent is still an indirection for trivial lookups, and for the end-to-end questions it loses the parallel coverage that made the tool useful. It trades the working case for a modest improvement on the failing one.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Before expanding your codebase Q&A agent from one team to the whole engineering org, leadership asks for proof it works. The proposed metric is median time-to-answer, currently 40 seconds, plus a thumbs-up button. In a spot check, 3 of 15 confident answers pointed to functions that no longer exist after a refactor, and all three had a thumbs-up. How should agent quality be evaluated?

options.text: Add "cite file and line for every claim" to the system prompt and track what share of answers include citations as the quality metric.
options.explanation: Citations improve answers but their presence is not correctness; the three wrong answers could each have cited a stale location. Measuring citation rate rewards the form of grounding without checking whether the grounding is true.

options.text: Replace the thumbs-up with a five-point rating and require a comment, so engineers provide richer signal on each answer.
options.explanation: Engineers rated the wrong answers positively because they did not know the code; a finer scale asks the same uninformed judge for more precision. It adds friction and still cannot detect confident errors in unfamiliar code.

options.text: Build a set of real questions with verified answers in the current repo, grade the agent against it, and re-run after prompt or model changes.
options.explanation: Only a ground-truth set can tell a confident wrong answer from a right one, which is exactly what the spot check found and the thumbs-up missed. It also makes quality a regression test, so later prompt or model changes are checked rather than assumed. Speed and satisfaction can be tracked alongside, not instead.

options.text: Log every tool call and have a second Claude session judge whether the agent explored enough of the repository before it answered each question.
options.explanation: Exploration depth is a process metric with no ground truth; an agent can read many files and still cite a deleted function. A model judge without verified answers reproduces the original problem one level up.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: You built an agent that tidies the issue tracker weekly through MCP tools (list_issues, add_comment, close_issue): it closes issues with no activity for 90 days. Last run it closed 212 issues, including 9 whose latest comment said "keep open, blocked on vendor" and 2 flagged as compliance items. Closing is reversible, but notifications already went to 60 stakeholders. What should change?

options.text: Make the run produce a proposed action list for a human to approve, then execute only the approved closures in a second step.
options.explanation: Bulk actions with external side effects are where a human gate pays for itself: reviewing a list of 212 candidates takes minutes, while unwinding notifications to 60 people cannot be done. Splitting propose from execute keeps the agent doing the work and the human doing the judgment, and it covers exclusion cases nobody has written down yet.

options.text: Add "do not close issues whose comments ask to keep them open or that carry compliance labels" to the agent's instructions.
options.explanation: This patches the two failure categories that were noticed and relies on the model applying them reliably. The next unwritten exception, an issue referenced by a live incident for example, leaks the same way, and the run still acts before anyone looks.

options.text: Have the agent add a warning comment and wait a week before closing, giving stakeholders a chance to object before the action.
options.explanation: Two hundred warning comments are themselves a mass notification, and the design shifts the review burden to every stakeholder rather than one operator. Issues nobody watches, which is most stale issues, still close without anyone deciding.

options.text: Lower the blast radius by capping each run at 25 closures, so a bad run affects fewer issues and can be reverted quickly.
options.explanation: A cap slows the damage but does not prevent it: the same wrong closures happen over nine weeks instead of one, each with its notifications. It also leaves the backlog growing while offering no mechanism for a person to catch the mistakes.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Your team built a weekly changelog agent: given Bash, Grep, and a GitHub MCP server, it is told to "gather last week's merged PRs, summarize them, and post to Slack". Some weeks it uses git log and misses squash-merge descriptions; other weeks it queries the MCP server and includes unmerged PRs; twice it posted before finishing. The summaries themselves are good. What should the design be?

options.text: Give the agent a detailed procedure in its system prompt: query the MCP server, filter by merged state and date, summarize, then post.
options.explanation: A procedure in the prompt is still executed by a model that may choose differently each week, which is the observed problem. It narrows the variance but the gathering step remains probabilistic when it has a single correct answer.

options.text: Split into a gathering subagent and a writing subagent so each has a narrow job and the coordinator checks the PR list before posting.
options.explanation: Adding agents to do deterministic work multiplies cost and coordination without removing the variability; the gathering subagent can still pick git log. The coordinator check is itself another model judgment about a list that code can produce exactly.

options.text: Add a PreToolUse hook on the Slack post tool that verifies the message references at least one PR before it is sent.
options.explanation: A hook can stop an empty or premature post but cannot know whether the PR set is complete or excludes unmerged work, which is where most of the errors came from. It guards one symptom and leaves the variability in the gathering step in place.

options.text: Fetch and filter the merged PRs in a script, call Claude once to write the summary, and post from the script; no agent loop.
options.explanation: The only step that benefits from a model is writing the summary, and that step already works. Gathering and posting have exact, testable definitions, so code does them the same way every week and cannot post early. Using an agent loop here bought variability and paid for it in cost and trust.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Engineers stopped using your SDK-based assistant after a week. Traces show it asked for confirmation on every action: 37 approval prompts in one session, 31 of them for Read, Grep, and Glob calls. The one time it ran git push --force to a shared branch it also asked, and the engineer, numbed by then, approved it. How should the permission design change?

options.text: Turn on auto-approval for all tools and rely on the git worktree isolation you already use so mistakes can be discarded.
options.explanation: A worktree contains local edits, but a force push leaves it and rewrites a shared remote; that is exactly the action that needs a deliberate yes. Auto-approving everything fixes the fatigue by removing the one prompt that mattered.

options.text: Auto-approve read-only tools and reserve confirmation for actions that change shared or external state, such as pushes and deletions.
options.explanation: Prompts should track reversibility, not tool count. Reads cannot cause harm, so approving them buys nothing and spends the engineer's attention; pushes and deletions are rare and consequential, so a prompt there is noticed. This makes the remaining confirmations meaningful, which is what makes them work.

options.text: Keep confirmation for every tool but batch the prompts so the engineer approves an entire plan at once rather than one call at a time.
options.explanation: Batching hides the dangerous call in a bundle of harmless ones, so the force push gets approved with the reads around it. It reduces clicks while making the one important decision less visible than before.

options.text: Ask for confirmation only on the first use of each tool per session, then remember the decision for the rest of the session.
options.explanation: The first Bash call is usually git status; approving it would silently approve the later force push. Per-tool memory conflates harmless and destructive uses of the same tool, which is precisely the distinction that matters.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Reviewers correct about 300 extracted records a day and the corrections are logged. An engineer proposes a nightly agent that reads the day's corrections, rewrites the extraction prompt and few-shot examples to address them, and deploys the new prompt before the morning batch, arguing that prompt edits are low-risk text changes. The pipeline processes 20,000 invoices a day into the ERP. How should this agent's autonomy be bounded?

options.text: Allow automatic deployment only when the rewrite changes fewer than 20 lines of the prompt, and route larger rewrites to an engineer for review.
options.explanation: Size is not risk: a one-word change to a field definition can shift 20,000 extractions a day, while a long rewrite of examples may be harmless. A line threshold gives the appearance of a boundary without measuring the thing that matters, which is the effect on extraction quality.

options.text: Deploy automatically but keep the previous prompt available, and roll back if the next day's reviewer overturn rate rises above the trailing average.
options.explanation: This uses a day of production as the test bed: a regressed prompt sends wrong records into the ERP before the signal arrives, and overturn rate lags because reviewers see only the sampled share of records. Rollback limits the duration of damage, not its occurrence.

options.text: Let the agent propose changes and score them on the labelled evaluation set; a human promotes a prompt only when scores hold or improve.
options.explanation: Generating candidate prompt changes from corrections is a good use of the agent; deploying them is a production change to a system feeding an ERP. Scoring each candidate against the labelled evaluation set turns the decision into evidence, and requiring a human to promote keeps the deployment boundary where the consequence lives. The agent does the work; it does not own the release.

options.text: Do not automate it; have engineers rewrite the prompt monthly from a summary of corrections, since prompt changes need human judgement.
options.explanation: Refusing the automation throws away the useful part, which is turning 300 daily corrections into concrete candidate fixes, and lets systematic errors persist for weeks. The concern is real but is addressed by gating the deployment, not by removing the agent.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your extraction agent submits validated invoices to the ERP with submit_record and also holds a create_vendor tool intended for genuinely new suppliers. When the ERP rejects a submission with vendor_not_found, traces show the agent calling create_vendor with the name as extracted and resubmitting successfully. Finance found 43 duplicate vendor records in a month, such as "ACME Corp." beside "Acme Corporation", each with its own payment history. What should change?

options.text: Remove create_vendor from the agent's tools; on vendor_not_found it stops and routes the record to a human with the extracted name and the closest matches.
options.explanation: Creating master data is a business decision with lasting consequences, and the agent was given a tool that let it treat an ERP rejection as an obstacle to route around. Removing the tool makes the rejection a stop condition: the agent hands over the evidence a human needs to pick the existing vendor or create a new one deliberately. Genuinely new suppliers are rare enough to be handled that way.

options.text: Keep the tool but instruct the agent to call create_vendor only after confirming that no vendor with a similar name already exists in the master list.
options.explanation: A prompt rule leaves the decision with the model and depends on it judging name similarity reliably every time; "ACME Corp." versus "Acme Corporation" is exactly the judgement it already got wrong. The tool that caused the damage stays available whenever the rule is not followed.

options.text: Make create_vendor perform a server-side fuzzy match and return existing candidates instead of creating when similarity exceeds 0.8, so duplicates are caught in the tool.
options.explanation: Fuzzy matching in the tool catches some duplicates, but a threshold will still split vendors with different legal names and merge distinct ones, and the agent remains empowered to create records whenever the match falls below it. It hardens the tool without asking whether the agent should hold it.

options.text: Add a second Claude call that must approve every create_vendor request by reviewing the extracted name against the vendor list before the tool executes.
options.explanation: A second model call adds cost and a false sense of a checkpoint: it reads the same extracted name with the same knowledge gaps and no ground truth about whether the supplier is new. Model-approves-model is not a human in the loop, and duplicates below its notice still get created.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your extraction agent holds both extraction tools and a submit_to_erp tool in one loop. When the ERP returns a transient 503, the agent sometimes re-extracts the document, gets a slightly different record, and submits again; the ERP now holds 140 near-duplicate purchase orders from one week. Retrying is appropriate; duplicates are not. How should the boundary be drawn?

options.text: Instruct the agent to retry submit_to_erp with the identical record on a 503 and never re-run extraction after a submission attempt.
options.explanation: This describes the right behaviour but leaves enforcement to the model inside the same loop that produced the duplicates. Under an error it may still reason its way back to extraction, and there is nothing structural to stop the second submission.

options.text: End the agent's job at a validated record; have deterministic code submit it with an idempotency key and handle retries.
options.explanation: Submission is a side-effecting operation with a known retry policy, so it belongs in code that retries the same payload under one idempotency key. The agent's competence is producing a correct record; stopping it there removes the path from a 503 back to re-extraction entirely, rather than asking it to avoid that path.

options.text: Make submit_to_erp idempotent by hashing the record contents so identical resubmissions are rejected by the ERP.
options.explanation: The duplicates were not identical; re-extraction produced slightly different records, so content hashes differ and pass. Idempotency keyed on content protects against exact repeats, not against the agent regenerating the record.

options.text: Add a check_existing_order tool the agent must call before submitting so it can detect a duplicate it created earlier.
options.explanation: Matching near-duplicates is itself a judgment call the agent can get wrong, and it adds turns to every document to defend against a problem created by letting the agent own submission. It treats the symptom while keeping the loop that causes it.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your extraction agent can call route_to_human when a document is ambiguous. Operations set a target of escalating no more than 5% of documents. The agent escalated 11%, a prompt tweak brought it to 4%, and the team is ready to ship. A reviewer notes that in the 4% run, two contracts with contradictory termination clauses went straight to the downstream system. How should escalation behaviour be evaluated?

options.text: Set the target as a range, for example 4 to 8 percent, so the prompt cannot be tuned so low that ambiguous documents slip through unnoticed.
options.explanation: A rate says nothing about which documents were escalated. An agent can sit inside any range while escalating easy documents and passing contradictory ones; the range makes the number look considered without measuring the decisions behind it.

options.text: Sample 50 escalated documents weekly and count how many reviewers judged genuinely ambiguous, driving the rate down only while that share stays high.
options.explanation: This measures escalation precision, whether escalated documents deserved it, and is worth doing. But the reported failure is a miss: documents that should have been escalated and were not, which a sample drawn only from escalations can never observe.

options.text: Label a document set for whether escalation was warranted, then measure both unnecessary and missed escalations against it before tuning the prompt.
options.explanation: Escalation is a classification decision and needs both error types measured: over-escalation costs reviewer time, under-escalation lets contradictory contracts through. A labelled set exposes the trade the prompt tweak actually made and lets the team tune toward correct decisions instead of toward a rate.

options.text: Track downstream correction rates: if the systems receiving the records report few manual fixes, the escalation rate is low enough to ship.
options.explanation: Downstream corrections are a lagging and partial signal; a contradictory termination clause may not surface until a dispute months later, and many errors are never traced back. It also cannot tell an escalation miss from an extraction error.

questions.scenario: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.question: Your team's internal MCP server exposes a run_sql tool so Claude Code can inspect the staging database while debugging. The description says "read-only: SELECT statements only", yet last week a session ran UPDATE orders SET status='shipped' while fixing a failing test, and a WITH ... DELETE statement slipped past a keyword check you added afterwards. Developers still need ad-hoc queries during debugging. What is the most robust design change?

options.text: Add a PreToolUse hook that rejects any run_sql input containing UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT or DROP before it reaches the server.
options.explanation: A hook is deterministic, but it is still a keyword filter over SQL text, which is exactly what the WITH ... DELETE statement already defeated; comments, string literals and stored procedures offer more bypasses. It also runs on each developer's machine, so anyone without the hook configured has an unguarded tool.

options.text: Expand the tool description with explicit examples of allowed and forbidden statements, and repeat the read-only rule in the project CLAUDE.md.
options.explanation: Descriptions and CLAUDE.md guidance shape what Claude tends to do, not what it can do. The session that ran UPDATE already had a description saying SELECT only; more words make the violation rarer, not impossible, which is not enough for a write to a shared database.

options.text: Run queries on a database role granted only SELECT, and rename the tool query_staging_readonly so the name states the limit.
options.explanation: Enforcing read-only at the database role makes the constraint hold regardless of what SQL the model writes or which client calls the server, and an UPDATE simply fails with a permissions error the model can read. The name reinforces the intent for tool selection, but the guarantee comes from the server side, not from the model's compliance.

options.text: Add mcp__internal__run_sql to the permissions.deny list in .claude/settings.json and have developers run queries by hand.
options.explanation: Denying the tool removes the write risk by removing the debugging capability the team said it still needs, so every database check becomes a manual copy-paste step. A read-only role keeps the tool useful while achieving the same safety, so this trades away value for no additional protection.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Your codebase-exploration agent uses an MCP tool search_symbols(name) backed by your indexing service. When an engineer asks where UserId is used, the tool returns 4,200 matches as one JSON array of roughly 380 KB, the turn takes 40 seconds, and the agent's answer cites three files and misses the rest. The index itself is accurate. How should the tool's contract change?

options.text: Return at most 50 matches by default, include the total count and a truncated flag, and accept offset and path_prefix parameters for narrowing.
options.explanation: Capping the page, reporting the true total and offering narrowing parameters lets the agent see the shape of the result, decide whether to page or filter by directory, and keep each turn small. The model gets a usable signal (4,200 total, 50 shown) instead of a wall of matches it cannot attend to.

options.text: Keep returning every match so the model has complete information, but call search_symbols from a subagent whose context is separate from the main conversation.
options.explanation: Isolating the call in a subagent protects the main conversation, but the subagent now receives the same 380 KB and has the same attention problem, so its summary will still miss files. The 40-second turn is also unchanged, and the token cost is paid every time the tool runs.

options.text: Have the indexing service summarise the matches with a second model call and return a prose overview of where the symbol is used.
options.explanation: A prose summary discards the exact paths and line numbers the agent needs to open files with Read or follow up with Grep, adds another model call to every search, and hides which matches were dropped. Exploration tools should return precise, structured data the model can act on.

options.text: Return the full match list compressed to file path and line number only, dropping code snippets so the response fits in fewer tokens.
options.explanation: Trimming snippets shrinks each entry but still ships 4,200 items in one result, so the response remains tens of thousands of tokens the model cannot reason over reliably. It also removes the context that lets the agent judge relevance without opening every file, without adding any way to narrow the search.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: A repetitive-task automation in your productivity agent opens pull requests through an MCP tool open_pr(branch, title, body). On Tuesday the GitHub call timed out after the PR had in fact been created; the agent retried and the team received two identical PRs, and a later retry produced a third. Roughly 2% of calls hit this timeout. Which change eliminates the duplicate PRs most reliably?

options.text: Instruct the agent in its system prompt to call list_prs for the branch before every open_pr and skip creation when one already exists.
options.explanation: This depends on the model remembering an extra step on every retry, including after a confusing timeout, and it adds a round trip to the 98% of calls that succeed. Duplicate protection is a property the tool should guarantee, not a convention the agent is asked to follow.

options.text: Return is_error: true with "PR already exists for this branch" when the server finds an open PR, so the agent stops retrying.
options.explanation: Rejecting the duplicate stops the third PR but leaves the agent holding an error with no PR number or URL, so it has to interpret the failure and work out how to continue. The successful outcome already exists; reporting it as an error turns a recoverable retry into a dead end.

options.text: Split the tool into push_branch and create_pr so a timeout in one step can be retried without repeating the other.
options.explanation: Finer steps do not change the failure: a timeout on create_pr after GitHub has created the PR still leads to a duplicate on retry. It also doubles the number of calls and gives the model a second partial-failure state to reason about.

options.text: Make open_pr idempotent on branch: return the existing open PR for that branch if there is one, otherwise create it and return it.
options.explanation: With the branch as the natural idempotency key, a retry after a timeout returns the PR that was already created, so repeated calls converge on one result and the agent always receives the PR it needs to continue. The guarantee lives in the tool, where it holds for every caller and every retry.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Your agent queries the internal issue tracker through an MCP tool search_issues(query: string). The description documents a mini-syntax such as status:open assignee:@me label:backend. Logs show Claude producing status=open, is:open, plain phrases like "open backend issues", and inconsistent quoting of labels, so about a third of searches return nothing and the agent reports that no matching issues exist. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add three worked examples of correctly formatted queries to the tool description and repeat the syntax rules in the agent's system prompt.
options.explanation: Examples improve the hit rate, but the model is still asked to generate a bespoke query language from memory on every call, and the drift you already see (is:open borrowed from GitHub syntax) is the predictable result. The schema can express these constraints so no generation is needed.

options.text: Replace the string with typed parameters: status as an enum, assignee, a labels array, and an optional free-text text field.
options.explanation: Typed parameters move the syntax into the input schema, where the enum and array types constrain what Claude can produce and the server owns the translation into the tracker's query language. The model expresses intent as fields it already understands rather than reproducing a formatting convention.

options.text: Have the server parse incoming queries leniently, accepting =, : and is: forms and mapping plain English to filters with a keyword table.
options.explanation: A forgiving parser papers over the current variants but must be extended every time a new phrasing appears, and it guesses silently: "open backend issues" could mean a label or a component. Ambiguous parses return wrong results that look like real searches, which is harder to detect than an empty one.

options.text: Return is_error: true with the expected syntax whenever the query fails to parse, so the model corrects its format on the next call.
options.explanation: Most of the bad queries do not fail to parse; they parse into filters that match nothing, so the server has no error to raise. Where it can detect a problem, this still costs an extra round trip per search and keeps the model responsible for a format it keeps getting wrong.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tooling on the Claude Agent SDK: helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate, and automate repetitive tasks — using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.question: Your platform team maintains a 12-step "explain this legacy service" walkthrough: locate entry points, map data stores, list scheduled jobs, and so on, parameterised by service name. Most engineers use Claude Code, but several use other MCP-capable clients, and the team wants the walkthrough started deliberately by the engineer with the service name supplied, not chosen by the model partway through a task. Where should this live in your MCP server?

options.text: As a tool explain_service(service_name) whose result is the 12-step instruction text, so any connected client can call it.
options.explanation: Tools are model-controlled: Claude decides when to call them, which is the opposite of the deliberate, engineer-initiated start the team wants, and it may invoke the walkthrough mid-task or never. Returning instructions as a tool result also blurs the line between data the model reads and directions it follows.

options.text: As a resource at legacy://walkthrough containing the steps, which engineers attach to the conversation when they need it.
options.explanation: Resources are application-controlled content such as documents or schemas; they carry no arguments, so the service name cannot be supplied and the steps cannot be tailored. Engineers would attach a generic document and then explain in chat which service they mean.

options.text: As a slash command in .claude/commands/explain-service.md that reads the service name from $ARGUMENTS.
options.explanation: A project slash command gives Claude Code users exactly the invocation you want, but it is a Claude Code feature and does nothing for the engineers on other MCP clients. The team asked for one definition that every client can use, which points at the MCP server rather than a per-client file.

options.text: As an MCP prompt with a required service_name argument that the engineer selects explicitly in their client.
options.explanation: MCP prompts are user-controlled templates with typed arguments, designed for exactly this case: a reusable, parameterised workflow the person chooses to start. Any MCP client can list and invoke it, and Claude Code surfaces server prompts as slash commands, so the one definition serves both groups.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your extraction service registers tools extract_invoice, extract_invoice_v2, and extract_invoice_strict because two schema generations were kept during a migration. The descriptions of the older two say "deprecated, prefer extract_invoice_strict", yet in 11% of runs Claude still calls extract_invoice_v2, producing records the downstream loader rejects. Claude also needs queue_human_review for unreadable scans. What is the right fix?

options.text: Remove extract_invoice and extract_invoice_v2 from the tools array, leaving the strict variant and queue_human_review.
options.explanation: A tool the model must never choose should not be offered: three near-identical extractors are a selection problem no description can fully solve, and removing them makes the wrong call impossible while leaving queue_human_review available. The deprecated code can stay on the server for other callers without appearing in this request.

options.text: Force tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice_strict"} so every request is guaranteed to produce a strict-schema record.
options.explanation: Forcing a single named tool guarantees the strict schema but also removes Claude's ability to call queue_human_review, so unreadable scans are forced into fabricated records instead of being routed to a person. It fixes the 11% by breaking the escalation path.

options.text: Move the deprecation warning to the top of the system prompt in capital letters and add two examples of choosing the strict variant.
options.explanation: Stronger wording and examples lower the misroute rate but keep offering the model three tools whose names and schemas overlap heavily, so some fraction of calls will still land on extract_invoice_v2. Prompt emphasis is the tool for nuanced choices, not for a tool that has no valid use.

options.text: Keep all three tools but have the server map extract_invoice_v2 outputs into the strict schema before returning them to the loader.
options.explanation: A server-side mapping keeps a translation layer alive indefinitely and cannot supply fields the v2 schema never captured, so the loader still receives incomplete strict records. It also spends engineering effort preserving a path the team has already decided nobody should take.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your invoice extraction tool's input schema defines line_items as a single string described as "JSON array of items, each with description, quantity, unit_price". Validation logs show 9% of outputs fail downstream parsing: unescaped quotes, quantities such as "2 pcs", and several items collapsed into one entry. Every call still counts as schema-valid because the field is just a string. How should the schema change?

options.text: Split the extraction: extract_invoice_header for top-level fields and extract_line_item called once per item so each item is checked on its own.
options.explanation: One call per line item multiplies round trips on long invoices, leaves the model to track which items it has already emitted, and makes reassembly and ordering the application's problem. The schema can express repeated typed items directly without turning one extraction into a dozen.

options.text: Keep the string field but expand its description with a complete example and rules for escaping quotes and using numeric quantities.
options.explanation: A richer description leaves the model hand-serialising JSON inside a JSON string, so escaping mistakes and "2 pcs" remain possible and remain invisible to schema validation. The instructions describe a structure the schema could enforce instead.

options.text: Define line_items as an array of objects with required description (string), quantity (number) and unit_price (number) properties.
options.explanation: Nested typed objects put the structure where the model already produces structured output: each item becomes a separate element, quantity must be a number, and quoting is handled by the tool-use encoding rather than by hand. The 9% of malformed strings disappear because there is no string to malform.

options.text: Add a validate_line_items tool that Claude calls after extraction to parse the string and report problems so it can retry.
options.explanation: A validation tool detects the bad strings after they are produced and adds a repair loop to every extraction, when the goal is to prevent them. It also relies on the model choosing to call it and to interpret the parse errors correctly, which is more model behaviour to trust, not less.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your extraction agent is given helper tools normalize_date, normalize_currency, and sum_line_items alongside the record_invoice extraction tool. Traces show a typical invoice takes 14 to 20 tool calls and about 35 seconds, mostly Claude converting each date and amount one at a time before finally calling record_invoice. Accuracy on the raw values it reads from the document is already high. What is the best redesign?

options.text: Keep the helper tools but instruct Claude to batch all values into one call per helper and to issue those three calls in parallel to cut the round trips.
options.explanation: Batching and parallel calls reduce the count from 14 to perhaps 4, but the model is still orchestrating deterministic conversions it does not need to see, and whether it actually batches is a behaviour you are asking for rather than guaranteeing. The pipeline stays slower and more variable than it has to be.

options.text: Remove the helper tools: have record_invoice capture dates and amounts as written, then normalise and reconcile totals in application code.
options.explanation: Date parsing, currency normalisation and summing are deterministic and need no judgement, so they belong in code after extraction, not in the model's loop. The agent does the one thing it is good at, reading the document accurately, in a single tool call, and the 35-second, 20-call trace collapses to one turn.

options.text: Merge the three helpers into one normalize_record tool that takes the whole draft record and returns it cleaned in a single round trip.
options.explanation: One combined helper is better than three, but it still asks the model to produce a draft, wait for the cleaned version, and then call record_invoice, so every invoice pays two extra turns for work that could run after the model has finished. The tool exists only because normalisation was put in the wrong place.

options.text: Enable prompt caching on the system prompt and tool definitions so the repeated tool-call turns become cheaper to run.
options.explanation: Caching lowers the input-token cost of each of the 14 to 20 turns but does nothing about their number or the 35 seconds of latency, which is the problem the traces show. It is a sensible optimisation for the pipeline you end up with, not a fix for the design that produces so many turns.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.question: Your extraction agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, calls submit_record to push validated invoices into the payables system without a person in the loop. Finance now requires human sign-off for any invoice whose total_amount exceeds 50,000 before it is submitted, while smaller invoices must keep flowing automatically. Auditors treat the rule as a hard control, not a preference. How should you implement it?

options.text: State the threshold in the system prompt and tell Claude to call queue_human_review instead of submit_record whenever total_amount is over 50,000.
options.explanation: A prompt rule is followed most of the time, and auditors need it followed every time; one large invoice submitted on a lapse is a control failure. Instructions belong alongside the enforcement so Claude understands why a call was blocked, but they cannot be the enforcement.

options.text: Add a required approved_by parameter to submit_record and have Claude populate it from the approval field on the document.
options.explanation: A required parameter only guarantees the field is present, not that a real approval happened: the model can fill it from any name it finds, or from nothing, to satisfy the schema. It also puts the sign-off decision inside the extraction call rather than in front of it.

options.text: Split into submit_record and submit_high_value_record, and leave the second out of the allowed tools so Claude cannot submit large invoices.
options.explanation: The model still decides which tool to call based on the amount, so a large invoice routed to submit_record goes straight through. Splitting tools moves the choice around without removing it from the model, and the missing tool gives no path to approval.

options.text: Intercept submit_record with a PreToolUse hook that reads total_amount from the input and denies the call above 50,000.
options.explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs in code before the tool executes and sees the exact input Claude supplied, so the threshold is enforced deterministically on every call regardless of what the model intended. Invoices under the limit pass untouched, larger ones are denied with a reason the agent can act on, and the control is auditable.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: Your PR review job runs claude -p on a GitHub Actions runner with a fresh checkout. Locally the same prompt runs npm test and cites failing tests in its findings, but CI reviews report that the suite could not be executed and the job log shows the Bash call was denied. The developer who set this up had allowed Bash(npm test:*) in .claude/settings.local.json. What is the right fix?

options.text: Run the CI invocation with --dangerously-skip-permissions so the review can execute whatever commands it decides are needed on the ephemeral runner.
options.explanation: Skipping permissions removes every guardrail, not just the one blocking npm test: the review job could run git push, delete files, or exfiltrate the runner's secrets. An ephemeral runner does not protect the repository token it holds. A single scoped allow rule solves the problem without opening that surface.

options.text: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md stating that Claude is permitted to run npm test during reviews and should do so before reporting findings.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md instructs the model; it does not grant permissions. The denial in the log comes from the harness's permission system, which in non-interactive mode rejects any tool call not covered by an allow rule. Claude already wants to run the tests; telling it again changes nothing about what the harness lets through.

options.text: Move the Bash(npm test:*) allow rule into the committed .claude/settings.json so every checkout, including the runner, carries it.
options.explanation: settings.local.json is gitignored and personal, so the runner's fresh checkout never sees the rule. The committed .claude/settings.json is the project-scoped, version-controlled layer: the same narrow rule then applies on every machine, is visible in review, and grants nothing beyond running the test suite.

options.text: Install a user-level ~/.claude/settings.json on the runner image with the allow rule, keeping the repository's settings files untouched.
options.explanation: A rule baked into the runner image works until someone rebuilds the image or switches runner pools, and it is invisible to anyone reading the repository. It also leaks the allow rule to every other repository that job image builds. The project's own settings file is where a project-specific permission belongs.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: A developer added a Stop hook to the committed .claude/settings.json that runs afplay /System/Library/Sounds/Glass.aiff so they hear a chime when Claude finishes. The CI review job runs claude -p on Linux runners, and every run now logs afplay: command not found from the hook. The same file holds a PostToolUse hook that runs eslint --fix, which the team wants in both CI and local sessions. Where should the chime hook live?

options.text: In the developer's user-level ~/.claude/settings.json, leaving the shared PostToolUse lint hook in the committed project settings.
options.explanation: Hooks follow the same scope hierarchy as other settings: user-level settings apply to that person on every project, while the committed project file is for behaviour the whole team and CI should share. A personal chime is a per-machine preference, so it belongs in ~/.claude/settings.json; the lint hook stays committed and keeps running in CI.

options.text: Keep it in the project file but wrap the command in if [ -z "$CI" ] so the hook body is skipped whenever the job runs on a CI runner.
options.explanation: The guard silences the CI error but leaves a macOS-only personal preference in a file every teammate and runner loads, and a Linux teammate will hit the same failure locally. It also solves a scoping problem with shell conditionals instead of the settings hierarchy that exists for exactly this.

options.text: Move both hooks into .claude/settings.local.json, which is gitignored, so hooks only execute on the machine that defines them.
options.explanation: settings.local.json is per-checkout and gitignored, so moving the lint hook there removes it from CI and from every other developer's clone; the team wanted that hook everywhere. Only the chime is personal, and it should move alone.

options.text: Pass --settings ci-settings.json on the CI invocation with a hooks block that contains only the lint hook, overriding the committed file.
options.explanation: --settings loads additional settings that are merged with the project and user files rather than replacing them, and hooks from every loaded scope run. The committed chime hook would still fire on the runner, and the workflow gains a second config file to maintain.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: The repository's committed .mcp.json defines a Postgres server and a Figma server that developers use locally; both need credentials that exist only on laptops. The CI review job needs one different server, an internal PR-metadata MCP server, and its logs show startup failures for the two developer servers on every run before the review begins. How do you configure MCP for the CI invocation?

options.text: Remove the two developer servers from .mcp.json and have each developer re-add them with claude mcp add --scope local on their own machine.
options.explanation: This breaks the shared configuration the stem says is working for developers. Local scope is per-user and per-machine, so six developers end up with six drifting setups and new joiners get nothing, all to fix a problem that only exists in one CI invocation.

options.text: Add the PR-metadata server to .mcp.json as a third entry and set the Postgres and Figma credentials to dummy values in the workflow environment.
options.explanation: Dummy credentials do not stop the two servers from starting and failing on every run; they just change the error. It also exposes the internal PR-metadata server to every developer session where it has no purpose and may lack the network access it needs.

options.text: Set enableAllProjectMcpServers to false in the committed .claude/settings.json so project servers are skipped until approved.
options.explanation: That setting governs whether project servers are auto-approved for everyone who clones the repo, so flipping it changes developer sessions too. It also does nothing to supply the PR-metadata server CI actually needs, and approval is an interactive step a headless job cannot perform.

options.text: Invoke claude -p with --mcp-config ci-mcp.json --strict-mcp-config so only the PR-metadata server is loaded in CI.
options.explanation: --mcp-config supplies a CI-specific server file and --strict-mcp-config tells Claude Code to load only those servers, ignoring .mcp.json and user-level configs. The developer servers never start in CI, the shared file stays untouched, and the CI server lives with the workflow.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.question: Your CI job asks Claude Code to generate unit tests for changed modules and commit them to the PR branch. About a third of runs produce test files that fail the repository's ESLint config (unused imports, forbidden any), and the separate lint stage then fails the pipeline after Claude has finished. CLAUDE.md already says 'run eslint on files you create'. What most reliably yields lint-clean tests?

options.text: Strengthen the CLAUDE.md instruction to say the lint step is mandatory and enumerate the rules that generated tests most often violate.
options.explanation: The instruction already exists and is skipped a third of the time; wording it more firmly keeps the check dependent on the model remembering to act. Listing rules helps a little with content but does nothing to guarantee the lint run happens on each file Claude writes.

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write that runs ESLint on the touched file and exits 2 so violations are fed back to Claude.
options.explanation: A PostToolUse hook runs deterministically after every file write, and exit code 2 returns the linter's stderr to Claude as feedback it must address before moving on. Lint becomes a guaranteed part of the loop rather than an instruction, and errors are fixed while the file is still in focus.

options.text: Move the lint stage ahead of Claude's step and include its output in the generation prompt so Claude sees which rules the codebase enforces.
options.explanation: Linting the existing code before generation reports on files Claude has not written yet, so it produces little to include and nothing about the tests to come. The failures happen in new files, and this ordering still leaves them unchecked until after Claude has finished.

options.text: Add a Stop hook that runs ESLint across the repository and aborts the job with a non-zero status when violations are found.
